                        <p>Later, my grandmother offered me the updated version the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amstrad_CPC#CPC_6128" rel="noopener">CPC6128</a> with the same RAM, but with a 3-inch floppy disk.</p>
                        <p>After that I had many other ones. I started to build them. I tried my first Linux distro in 1995. It was a Debian. Today, my main distribution is still Debian, even if I tried, and used many others.</p>
                        <p>I've tried probably many window managers over the years. But, for the last 15 years more or less, I've been using only <a href="https://awesomewm.org" rel="noopener">awesomewm</a>, a tiling window manager, light, and customizable if you know Lua a bit.</p>
                        <p>I could write a lot about Linux, but I don't think it'd be of much interest to our readers. What I can say is that my love for computers is what got me to where I am today in my career.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>What's the story behind your blog?</h3>
                        <p>My first blog was about Debian, the GNU/Linux distribution. It was in 2001, and it was called debianworld.org. I used to write how-tos, and articles about Linux. I used the blog to post English to French translation of the Debian Weekly News, but also the <strong>Securing Debian Manual</strong>, and some part of the <strong>Advanced Bash scripting guide</strong>. Then in 2014, after a long summer, I found out I got cyber squatted. And, just like this it was gone.</p>
                        <p>Then, for five years, I didn't set up anything online until 2019. I met a colleague that asked me if I participated in any conferences, or if I had a blog. That's when I wanted to have a personal place online again.</p>
                        <p>I love bears, that's why I chose that domain name. And, lazy, because I am sometimes.</p>
                        <p>About the theme, it took me some time to create it, and be happy with the final result. But, then, it didn't really change.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>What does your creative process look like when it comes to blogging?</h3>
                        <p>It depends. First, I need a topic, or an idea.</p>
                        <p>Sometimes a blog post, a news, a new tool, or basically anything can inspire me to write directly a post.</p>
                        <p>But, often, I like to go through my Zettelkasten.</p>
                        <p>Every morning, I use this keybinding &lt;Ctrl&gt;-0. That opens a random note. If it doesn't sparkle anything, I hit the same keys again. A <em>"new"</em> note appears, and, sometimes,  a <em>discussion</em> starts. I will add more content, or argue with previous thoughts. That's how some drafts start.</p>
                        <p>English not being my mother tongue, I read the different parts multiple times to be sure to make sense. My goal is to make simple sentences, but that connect with everyone.</p>
                        <p>Once done, I check if some grammar hasn't been forgotten by my LSP.</p>
                        <p>Then, a script will sync the content to my blog, and post it also on Mastodon.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Do you have an ideal creative environment? Also do you believe the physical space influences your creativity?</h3>
                        <p>I don't. I just need my laptop, a terminal, and a coffee. That's all.</p>
                        <p>Maybe the physical space could help some people. Maybe if I had a seaside view, it could impact my creativity &#128517;.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>A question for the techie readers: can you run us through your tech stack?</h3>
                        <p>Previously, for other projects, I used Drupal, then Wordpress. But, for this one, I wanted something easily to maintain. No database, or plugins updates. Something simple. That's why I went for a SSG, a Static Site Generator.</p>
                        <p>I chose <a href="https://gohugo.io" rel="noopener">Hugo</a>, and I've been happy with it for years.</p>
                        <p>There is some JavaScript from <a href="https://carlschwan.eu/2020/12/29/adding-comments-to-your-static-blog-with-mastodon/" rel="noopener">Carl Schwan's post</a> to add Mastodon's comment on the blog. So far it works well. Everything is hosted on a dedicated server.</p>
                        <p>All post have been written in Neovim, my go-to editor, on a Tuxedo laptop. My local repository has a backup on a Synology DS1812+ NAS, which also had a remote backup. That repository is pushed on a private Codeberg repository too.</p>
                        <p>Domain name was purchase at <a href="https://Unlimited.rs" rel="noopener">Unlimited.rs</a>, a registar in Serbia. Originally, the name of the blog was lazybear.io, but since the announcement that it will disappear in the future, that's when I switched to a Serbian one. For other projects, I use also Porkbun that I love.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Given your experience, if you were to start a blog today, would you do anything differently?</h3>
                        <p>I don't think so.</p>
                        <p>A few of my friends suggested that I should specialize and monetize it, but that was never its goal.</p>
                        <p>It's my little corner on the web where I can do whatever I want. I can tweak it as I want, try new things, post photos the way I want, without having to follow a specific format.</p>
                        <p>It was always meant to be my place to experiment.</p>
                        <p>I don't track visitors, I don't care about numbers.</p>
                        <p>Now, and then, I get some emails, and I like the discussions I get there. Keep them coming &#128588;</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Financial question since the Web is obsessed with money: how much does it cost to run your blog? Is it just a cost, or does it generate some revenue? And what's your position on people monetising personal blogs?</h3>
                        <p>The domain name is around &euro;24 per year. The dedicated server around &euro;30 per month, but I use it for other things too.</p>
                        <p>It doesn't generate any money. I could add a Ko-fi account, and maybe I will... just in case. &#128519;</p>
                        <p>If people want to monetize it, I don't see any issue with that. Everyone is free to do whatever they want.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Time for some recommendations: any blog you think is worth checking out? And also, who do you think I should be interviewing next?</h3>
                        <p>Ok, I have a couple of them!</p>
                        <ul>
                            <li><a href="https://rldane.space" rel="noopener">Rldane.space</a></li>
                            <li><a href="https://zerokspot.com" rel="noopener">Zerokspot.com</a></li>
                            <li><a href="https://joelchrono.xyz" rel="noopener">Joelchrono.xyz</a></li>
                            <li><a href="https://benjaminhollon.com" rel="noopener">Benjaminhollon.com</a></li>
                            <li><a href="https://christiantietze.de" rel="noopener">Christiantietze.de</a></li>
                        </ul>
                        <p>And, two French photographers:</p>
                        <ul>
                            <li><a href="https://Jeremyjanin.com" rel="noopener">Jeremyjanin.com</a></li>
                            <li><a href="https://GregoryMignard.com" rel="noopener">GregoryMignard.com</a></li>
                        </ul>
                        <p>I also have a <a href="https://lazybea.rs/links/" rel="noopener">list of blogs I enjoy, and follow</a>.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Final question: is there anything you want to share with us?</h3>
                        <p>Yeah start a blog, value your privacy, and send an email to Manuel so we can find more about you.</p>
                    </section>
                </section>

                <!-- Closing -->
                <p>&bull;--&#9825;--&bull;</p>

            </section>

      <pubDate>Fri, 01 May 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid isPermaLink="true">https://zacharykai.net/notes/pb/hyde</guid>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>People and Blogs: Nicolas Solerieu</title>
      <link>https://zacharykai.net/notes/pb/solerieu</link>
      <description>People and Blogs is a series by Manuel Moreale featuring the people behind personal blogs and the stories of their corners of the web. This conversation is with Nicolas Solerieu. Do go visit their blo...</description>
      <content:encoded><![CDATA[<section class="e-content">

                <!-- Introduction -->
                <p id="top" class="p-summary"><em><a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/pb" rel="noopener">People and Blogs</a> is a series by <a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/" rel="noopener">Manuel Moreale</a> featuring the people behind personal blogs and the stories of their corners of the web. This conversation is with Nicolas Solerieu. Do go visit <a href="https://slrncl.com/blog" rel="noopener">their blog</a> and say hello!</em></p>

                <!-- Interview -->
                <section>
                    <h2>Interview</h2>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Let's start from the basics: can you introduce yourself?</h3>
                        <p>I&rsquo;m dad, designer, cyclist, designer, texture guy &ndash; currently living in San Luis Obispo, CA. My oldest kid just learned to blow his nose. The other one is in his prime baby time. These days I day dream about <a href="https://bikepacking.com/" rel="noopener">bikepacking</a> and <a href="https://unsplash.com/s/photos/permaculture" rel="noopener">permaculture</a>.</p>
                        <p>Born and raised in France, I landed in California in 2016. An odd mix of work ethic and ego led me to define myself through the stuff I make: all sorts of combinations of rectangles and text boxes, mostly for screens, solely because I got good enough to get paid for it. While I'm filled with gratitude for my career, I spend a humorously uncomfortable amount of time torn between ascetic ideals and pragmatism.</p>
                        <p>While I&rsquo;m not a technologist, I&rsquo;m not a monk either. I&rsquo;m way too fidgety. Time outdoors, family life, movement, and occasional meditation keep me sane.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>What's the story behind your blog?</h3>
                        <p>I adopted this domain name in 2016 as I didn't like having my real name spelled out in the URL, it felt weird. I bought my initial domain back in 2012: <a href="http://nicolas-soleri.eu/" rel="noopener">nicolas-soleri.eu</a>, I thought it was clever. SLRNCL is a concatenation of my last name and my first name without the vowels. It's hard to remember, which is great since I'm not trying to play the SEO game.</p>
                        <p>I truly started to put effort into writing in 2022. The birth of my first child probably had a lot to do with it &ndash; and getting off instagram. I couldn&rsquo;t fathom the idea of being a dad with an instagram account. But I&rsquo;d love for my kids to one days read the blog of their silly dad.</p>
                        <p>Self-awareness and allergy to grandiosity creates a tension between craft, skepticism, and my embodied experience which I love to put into words. The blog-therapy is (still) working. It&rsquo;s eating up most of <a href="https://slrncl.com/blog/2025-12-01-the-ego-in-the-codebase" rel="noopener">my creative ego</a> and filling my feed.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>What does your creative process look like when it comes to blogging?</h3>
                        <p>Nowadays I use the default iOS notes app. I write whenever. I edit little.</p>
                        <p>I used to have a notes.txt file on my desktop where I was putting down all interesting nuggets, like a wine cellar, hoping for them to mature. Instead, they mostly degenerated and created a bunch of anxiety from doing nothing of it.</p>
                        <p>I breed an uncomfortably large amount of thoughts daily. Most of them are unexceptional. I cultivate poor writing hygiene because I do not want to truly get into writing. Yet, there seems to be something that keeps bringing me back to words. To tame my ego and avoid creating a generational supply of passable notes I use my blog as a graveyard.</p>
                        <p>Typos are my own, I&rsquo;m working on it. With AI it now feels like a mark of authenticity. Sometimes I ask my wife to proof-read, but that is rare because we end up arguing, worth it.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Do you have an ideal creative environment? Also do you believe the physical space influences your creativity?</h3>
                        <p>Following the flow of life is what makes my creative juice flow. I often write on the toilet or in public parks while keeping an eye on my kids. I thrive in &ldquo;white-space&rdquo; time - time in between things. So I jot down notes when I&rsquo;m out and about. I&rsquo;m not a coffee shop person and <a href="https://slrncl.com/blog/2025-07-01-breaking-up-with-my-office" rel="noopener">I hate my home office</a>.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>A question for the techie readers: can you run us through your tech stack?</h3>
                        <p>My website is home cooked. It runs mostly on PHP. I still have Jquery installed but I&rsquo;m slowly removing all Javascript dependencies. I'm not a great dev and prefer to stay 5 years behind trends. My website is constrained by my skills. This has kept me grounded and covered most of my needs and ambitions. I don't recommend inspecting my code, it's really not great but decently light. Building stuff is a great way to keep myself grounded in the process. I use Inter as the only font because it's nice, plain, and open source. It will default to system font if Inter isn't available. Because I don't want to import anything custom or use CDN. I'm not better than Inter (and few out there are IMO).</p>
                        <p>The site is hosted by OVH in France. I&rsquo;m considering self-hosting since my house produces excess solar power.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Given your experience, if you were to start a blog today, would you do anything differently?</h3>
                        <p>I&rsquo;d use bearblog if I was not a pretentious web designer and had to start over. I recommended it to <a href="https://soleliu.com/" rel="noopener">my wife</a>, she likes it. The simplicity and authenticity of the project is lovely. That said I do not regret the torturous process of having redesigned my website tirelessly over the last decade. The process taught me a lot about myself.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Financial question since the Web is obsessed with money: how much does it cost to run your blog? Is it just a cost, or does it generate some revenue? And what's your position on people monetising personal blogs?</h3>
                        <p>My domain name + hosting cost under 20 euros/year. I do not run ads or track anything - I don&rsquo;t plan or change this ever.</p>
                        <p>That means my website has had an incredible ROI considering the career opportunities it gave me. The many people who hired me all visited my website (and told me about it). I had some rewarding connections with internet strangers. My gratitude is larger than an html file can hold, and definitely magnitude greater than what it cost me to run my website.</p>
                        <p>Money is important, and I&rsquo;m a lucky bastard. I don&rsquo;t have anything against people monetizing their thoughts - though I&rsquo;m rarely compelled by a paywall. Digital patronage and crowdfunding seems highly relevant to get out of the social media hell realm of today. It has pitfalls, the main one being requiring mass adoption which seems highly delusional. But hope and compassion are contagious while big tech fights entropy. Social media always comes back in a different form, meanwhile, html is still there. It&rsquo;s the cockroach business model.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Time for some recommendations: any blog you think is worth checking out? And also, who do you think I should be interviewing next?</h3>
                        <ul>
                            <li>These two crack me up and make me think: <a href="https://gkeenan.co/" rel="noopener">Keenan</a> and <a href="https://taylor.town/" rel="noopener">Taylor town</a> (already seen on P&amp;B)</li>
                            <li>Some wholesome Aussie stories: <a href="https://beaumiles.com/" rel="noopener">Beau Miles</a></li>
                            <li><a href="https://maggieappleton.com/" rel="noopener">Maggie Appleton</a> always gets me interested</li>
                            <li>The only design blog <a href="https://vanschneider.com/blog/" rel="noopener">Tobias Van Shneider</a> I've ever read</li>
                            <li>I'm a fan of <a href="https://faircompanies.com/" rel="noopener">Faircompanies</a> stories and mission</li>
                            <li>Not a blog but worth checking out <a href="https://simplybeing.co.uk/audio-records-by-james/" rel="noopener">James low audio archive</a></li>
                        </ul>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Final question: is there anything you want to share with us?</h3>
                        <p>There are so many goodies out there, one link away. Sharing is fun, side projects too. In my case it took me a decade to get my head out of my own butt and realize the cost of my own ventures. I believe a lot of us are similar to me, moving through life and accumulating stuff. Cleaning up, giving up, and passing along are necessary processes. So as a closing thought I&rsquo;d suggest to sit, close your eyes and think of all your stuff. If you&rsquo;re comfortable with it, great. Otherwise, spring is coming.</p>
                    </section>
                </section>

                <!-- Closing -->
                <p>&bull;--&#9825;--&bull;</p>

            </section>
]]></content:encoded>
      <pubDate>Fri, 24 Apr 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid isPermaLink="true">https://zacharykai.net/notes/pb/solerieu</guid>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>People and Blogs: JTR</title>
      <link>https://zacharykai.net/notes/pb/jtr</link>
      <description>People and Blogs is a series by Manuel Moreale featuring the people behind personal blogs and the stories of their corners of the web. This conversation is with JTR. Do go visit their blog and say hel...</description>
      <content:encoded><![CDATA[<section class="e-content">

                <!-- Introduction -->
                <p id="top" class="p-summary"><em><a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/pb" rel="noopener">People and Blogs</a> is a series by <a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/" rel="noopener">Manuel Moreale</a> featuring the people behind personal blogs and the stories of their corners of the web. This conversation is with JTR. Do go visit <a href="https://taonaw.com" rel="noopener">their blog</a> and say hello!</em></p>

                <!-- Interview -->
                <section>
                    <h2>Interview</h2>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Let's start from the basics: can you introduce yourself?</h3>
                        <p>I go by JTR these days, which is based on an earlier pseudonym I picked up long ago. Sort of an alter ego I guess. I like how it rolls off the tongue, so I stuck with it. I was a writer (and a bit of a journalist) and a teacher before I found my way into IT. Today I&rsquo;m a sort of manager who still writes plenty of technical documentation and attends a lot of meetings.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>What's the story behind your blog?</h3>
                        <p>I had a few blogs in the past, but when I started working for the medical center which I'm still working for today, 8 years ago, I decided to record my quest to learn technology in a blog. Soon after I started there, I was looking for an app to write checklists and bullet points, and I found <a href="https://www.orgzly.com" rel="noopener">Orgzly</a>. It seemed minimal, and I liked that it just writes everything to text files. I had no idea what org-mode was (or Emacs for that matter), and after a few weeks with the app I was deep down in rabbit hole.</p>
                        <p>So the start of my current position, along with learning Emacs and org-mode gave me a boost to start blogging what I was learning. I think it was my boss back then or one of my co-workers who didn't understand why I couldn't just use one of the many note-taking apps that were already available to us. That question, along with my reputation of always asking many of my own whenever we had meetings, had me come up with the idea that I should just call my blog &ldquo;The Art of Not Asking Why,&rdquo; hinting at one of my favorite books, Zen And The Art of Motorcycle Maintenance. It was just organic like that. &ldquo;The Art of Not Asking Why&rdquo; is kind of long, so I started to abbreviate it with &ldquo;TAONAW&rdquo; (I pronounce it "Tao-Now"), and I liked how it sounded... so here we are.&rdquo;  (the name of the book should be all caps&hellip;)</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>What does your creative process look like when it comes to blogging?</h3>
                        <p>Today, my blog is a mix of quick thoughts and longer posts, both of which are handled well by design by Micro.blog, my blogging platform, which I&rsquo;m very happy with.  For short posts (300 characters or so, "tweets" and "toots" basically), I usually use my iPhone or Android.</p>
                        <p>Longer posts usually start in Emacs org-mode as a draft, and then are edited by hand before I pass them through Grammarly and/or AI for typos and various checks. AI is excellent to find broken links, technical terms that I might want to expand on ( and suggest links to those), and switching <em>back</em> to org-mode so that my draft ends up being updated with the same post, typo and error-free (or almost free) on my blog.</p>
                        <p>For screenshots, I use <a href="https://www.techsmith.com/snagit/" rel="noopener">SnagIt</a>, which is paid for by my job (I write plenty of technical documents). Snaggit is excellent, and I'd pay for it in a heartbeat myself if I had to. For photos, which I take with my Sony camera or iPhone, I use Apple Photos these days for light editing. I also have <a href="https://www.darktable.org/" rel="noopener">Darktable</a> and <a href="https://krita.org/en/" rel="noopener">Krita</a> on my Linux desktop, both of which are free, excellent tools that are highly underrated in my opinion. They give me all the power Adobe Photoshop and Lightroom used to give me, without costing me a dime and just make me feel good to use.</p>
                        <p>My posts usually come from different experiences I go through, technical or otherwise. Sometimes I look in my journal and modify an entry from there to a post, at other times I go to my old blog and import a post from there and add it to my blog with the original timeline, yet other times I got over my images and pages on my blog - there&rsquo;s always something to do, beyond just writing the posts. I think that&rsquo;s part of the fun. A good blog grows with you, and you learn to tell more about yourself as you progress.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Do you have an ideal creative environment? Also do you believe the physical space influences your creativity?</h3>
                        <p>I used to work from coffee shops, but today I mostly blog from home. My apartment is quiet and less distracting, and the best time for me to write is in the morning (if I have enough time available), so this combination usually wins me over. I need to focus when I write, and I don&rsquo;t like to get distracted, which is another reason why home is usually the best place. I absolutely love my noise-cancelling Sony WH-1000XM6 (and the WH-1000XM5 before those) headphones, which have been a life changer for me, a person who can get distracted when my neighbors from across the hall return home. My mechanical keyboard, a Kensis Freestyle Edge RGB, is about 7 years old now and I love the feel of the mechanical keys under my fingers. The ergonomic setup (it's a split keyboard) helps my wrists, and my standing desk helps my concentration further.  When I write, I also listen to music: electronic or classical. Songs with lyrics usually distract me.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>A question for the techie readers: can you run us through your tech stack?</h3>
                        <p>I have two computers. A MacBook Pro M2, and a System76 thelio <a href="https://taonaw.com/2025/01/11/system-thelio-mira-first-impressions.html" rel="noopener">mira</a>, currently running Kubuntu, which is also my gaming computer. From these two, I lean slightly toward using the Mac for my writing because I take most of my photos with my iPhone and the Micro.blog desktop app that I use is for macOS.</p>
                        <p>My blog is hosted on Micro.blog, which is a hybrid of a social platform and a blogging platform in one. Micro.blog uses Hugo to build the blog and Micropub for the social network. It also syndicates to other social networks like Tumblr and Medium and plenty more that I don't use. It&rsquo;s a rather unique place that follows the POSSE (Publish Own Site, Syndicate Elsewhere) <a href="https://indieweb.org/POSSE?from=fediverse" rel="noopener">principles</a>. I like the fact that I can download all of my data, which includes my posts, my media and my CSS/HTML templates, any time I wish and take them elsewhere. That&rsquo;s how the web should be. When I joined Micro.blog I had to register my own domain, which I did, but these days you can also get a domain through them, and I believe you can also get a certificate through Let&rsquo;s Encrypt in one go. It's a bit confusing at the start since the concepts of a social network and a blog (=website) are different aspects in our minds, but they don't have to be that separate.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Given your experience, if you were to start a blog today, would you do anything differently?</h3>
                        <p>No. What I know today and the tools I use are the best ones for me at this point. If anything, I&rsquo;d encourage myself to have learned to use Emacs much earlier and to have adhered to POSSE long ago; that would have saved me from losing work on Medium and Blogger, which are now long gone. I recommend micro.blog wholeheartedly.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Financial question since the Web is obsessed with money: how much does it cost to run your blog? Is it just a cost, or does it generate some revenue? And what's your position on people monetising personal blogs?</h3>
                        <p>My plan on Micro.blog (hosting) costs $100 a year, which isn't horrible when you break it down to $8 and change per month. Micro.blog comes with many additional tools (such as hosting podcasts, encrypted notes, storing videos and more) which are worth it in my opinion. My domain costs about $30 a year.</p>
                        <p>I absolutely hate how ads work on the internet today, and I will never have ads on my blog, but I believe it's OK to ask for support or, as I like to think of it, "tips." If someone likes something I wrote, they are welcome to leave a tip. I don't need it however to keep the blog going, thankfully.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Time for some recommendations: any blog you think is worth checking out? And also, who do you think I should be interviewing next?</h3>
                        <p>I don&rsquo;t have a long list, and I think most of the folks I know were already covered in this series. I will highlight a few that are more active:</p>
                        <ul>
                            <li><a href="https://anniemueller.com/" rel="noopener">Annie&rsquo;s blog</a>: she often writes essays about feelings and life experiences, about once a week or so.</li>
                            <li><a href="https://sals.place/" rel="noopener">Sal</a>: mostly tech, here and there some other life stuff</li>
                            <li><a href="https://www.thewanderinglensman.com/" rel="noopener">The Wandering Lensman</a> He's professional photographer, usually an image and a short text. I like what he says about taking photos.</li>
                            <li><a href="https://pluralistic.net/" rel="noopener">Pluralistic from Cory Doctorow</a> does this guy really need an intro&hellip;? I love how well-linked and resourced the daily essays are. An (the?) online privacy activist.</li>
                            <li><a href="https://daily.baty.net/" rel="noopener">Jack Baty Daily</a> I lose track if this is the &ldquo;real&rdquo; blog or not. The guy changes blogs and platforms like we change shirts. But that&rsquo;s part of the fun.</li>
                        </ul>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Final question: is there anything you want to share with us?</h3>
                        <p>I&rsquo;d love, love to see more non-techie folks on POSE-style blogs. I&rsquo;m not talking about Medium or Tumblr; these are Silos. Some exist, here and there. There used to a be a priod, back when people published on movable type and wordpress was still something new no one knew about, where I was following a diner waitress from Jersey, a fighter pilot who was a patriot in the good kind of way, and of course, there was the USS clueless (I think he&rsquo;s still around, in retirement). Now, you have to be in the industry to do anything like that. I had a conversation with my partner the other day and he just shrugged. The term &ldquo;silo&rdquo; (he uses Tumblr) is so regular now that it&rsquo;s like explaining water to a fish. And it&rsquo;s a shame. Those that are different, micro.blog included, seems to require some knowledge of what, I guess, used to be common knowledge if you wanted to be online. I don&rsquo;t know. Perhaps if I was still a teacher, I&rsquo;d teach these internet &ldquo;basics&rdquo; to teens.</p>
                    </section>
                </section>

                <!-- Closing -->
                <p>&bull;--&#9825;--&bull;</p>

            </section>
]]></content:encoded>
      <pubDate>Fri, 17 Apr 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid isPermaLink="true">https://zacharykai.net/notes/pb/jtr</guid>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>People and Blogs: Frank Meeuwsen</title>
      <link>https://zacharykai.net/notes/pb/meeuwsen</link>
      <description>People and Blogs is a series by Manuel Moreale featuring the people behind personal blogs and the stories of their corners of the web. This conversation is with Frank Meeuwsen. Do go visit their blog ...</description>
      <content:encoded><![CDATA[<section class="e-content">

                <!-- Introduction -->
                <p id="top" class="p-summary"><em><a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/pb" rel="noopener">People and Blogs</a> is a series by <a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/" rel="noopener">Manuel Moreale</a> featuring the people behind personal blogs and the stories of their corners of the web. This conversation is with Frank Meeuwsen. Do go visit <a href="https://blog.frankmeeuwsen.com" rel="noopener">their blog</a> and say hello!</em></p>

                <!-- Interview -->
                <section>
                    <h2>Interview</h2>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Let's start from the basics: can you introduce yourself?</h3>
                        <p>Hi, I'm Frank. A somewhat older, beardy, less grumpy digital Gen-X'er from Utrecht, the Netherlands. Since October 2025 I've been self-employed. I work as a trainer/coach/writer on using AI in a creative and responsible way and I help knowledge workers with their digital awareness, digital skills and personal knowledge management.</p>
                        <p>My whole career has been online. Since I stumbled on this internet-thing in 1993, graduated in 1996 and joined one of the first free Internet Service Providers in the Netherlands. We would now call it a startup. Back then we were cowboys doing crazy stuff.</p>
                        <p>In 1997 I started at an internet agency with two of my close friends. I left in 2009 to become self-employed, had some incredible adventures as a freelancer at the Utrecht University of Applied Sciences, telecom companies, publishing houses. An IoT startup brought me back into agency life, went bust in 2019, and I ended up back at my old agency for 6 years. In October 2025 I went solo again.</p>
                        <p>I live in Utrecht with my lovely wife and two kids. We are obedient to the true master of our family, Bowie the cat. We spend time reading, watching movies, visiting concerts, going on walks, playing D&amp;D as a family and mostly just chilling through our lives.</p>
                        <p>I recently became a member of the <a href="https://metalbc.com/home/" rel="noopener">Metal Business Club</a>. A business club for anyone who also likes their music loud. Which gives you an idea of my musical taste.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>What's the story behind your blog?</h3>
                        <p>In 2000 I stumbled upon a Dutch site from a guy who was just describing his day-to-day life. Sharing links, publishing short posts. I worked at an internet agency where we made our own CMS but I had never seen this thing called a blog. I clicked through on an orange button with the word <em>Blogger</em> on it, signed up, made <a href="http://web.archive.org/web/20150218113325/http://punkey.com/archives/archive_2000-m07.php" rel="noopener">my first post</a> of a site I just visited... and that was that. I was hooked. Even though we made CMS systems for our clients, it hadn't occurred to me I could do this myself. I didn't need an editorial team, a studio, a radio tower. I could just... blog. I named my first blog Punkey, which was my nickname on IRC in the years before. And that's how it all started.</p>
                        <p>I fully engaged in the Dutch blogosphere. Since it was so small, we all got to know each other pretty fast, also because of the meetups we organized at least once every six months or so. I got active in a Dutch online magazine called about:blank, where we wrote about the Dutch blogscene. We also hosted weblogawards called the <a href="https://www.wikiwand.com/nl/articles/Dutch_Bloggies" rel="noopener">Dutch Bloggies</a>.</p>
                        <p>In 2010 I wrote a book "Bloghelden" (Blog Heroes) about the history of the Dutch blogosphere. You can still <a href="https://bloghelden.nl/" rel="noopener">read it for free online</a> if your Dutch is OK.</p>
                        <p>My first blog <a href="http://web.archive.org/web/20150217022140/http://www.punkey.com/" rel="noopener">Punkey.com</a> lasted only five years, from July 2000 to July 2005. But after that I had plenty of other blogs:</p>
                        <p><strong>Frank-ly (2002 - 2009)</strong> was the first agency blog in the Netherlands. I started it, left the agency in 2009, the blog continued without me. It's no longer live. What does live on <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20060929174456/http://frank-ly.nl/twttr-oftewel-present-tense-blogging/" rel="noopener">is my infamous post from 2006</a> where I write off Twitter as a fad. One of my better mistakes.</p>
                        <p><strong>Whatsthenextaction (2004-2008)</strong> was my English-language blog on Getting Things Done. A forerunner in what later became the productivity blogging industry. At some point it got picked up by CNN and Time Magazine. <a href="http://web.archive.org/web/20080304054150/http://www.whatsthenextaction.com/" rel="noopener">Web Archive Link</a>.</p>
                        <p><strong>Lifehacking (2007-2015)</strong> is the one that still stings a little. With a growing group of authors we put this term on the Dutch map. I tried to turn it into a sustainable <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20150831074018/http://lifehacking.nl/" rel="noopener">online and offline publication</a>. That didn't work out the way I wanted. In 2015 the site and all the posts passed to new ownership.</p>
                        <p><strong>Digging the Digital (2014-2023)</strong> is the longest running <a href="https://diggingthedigital.com/" rel="noopener">blog</a> I had. I changed the plumbing a few times (Ghost, Jekyll, WordPress) and it's the blog where I wrote a lot about the indieweb and owning your own platform.</p>
                        <p><strong>Digging the Digital (2023 - present)</strong> Same name but a <a href="https://blog.frankmeeuwsen.com/" rel="noopener">different URL</a>. No more difficult titles (for now), just my name in the URL. Simple. WordPress became too heavy and too much for me. I wanted to get back to the basics of blogging, writing. Simple pieces of typing and not too difficult with themes, plugins and formatting. So I run everything on the great Micro.blog service.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>What does your creative process look like when it comes to blogging?</h3>
                        <p>It is not a really strict set of rules I follow. Actually, it never was. I always have a swipe-file with ideas in Obsidian, I've collected through the years. But to be honest, that's a big pile of files I hardly look at. Since 2025 I use <a href="https://sublime.app/?ref=frank" rel="noopener">Sublime</a> as an Idea Discovery Engine. Sublime is the lovechild of Pinterest and Obsidian. You can save links, texts, video, images, audio, podcast-snippets. Put them on a canvas, connect them, find related ideas from other Sublime users and mold your own thoughts. I love to use Sublime to find new ideas, connect them and use it as a jump-off point for my own writing.</p>
                        <p>Besides that, blogposts also appear when I just have a thought. Or something I see and want to respond to. So nothing fancy. Just writing.</p>
                        <p>Sometimes I have Claude Cowork interview me on a subject or idea and use <a href="https://hex.kitlangton.com/" rel="noopener">Hex</a> (open source speech to text tool) to talk it oud loud. The unfiltered mess that comes out goes into Obsidian, where I puzzle the pieces into an actual post. It's surprisingly effective for me.</p>
                        <p>I don't have AI write the post for me. I tried this in the past, it never worked out really well. The voice is off, the thinking isn't mine. AI helps me shape my thoughts, but I stay in the driver's seat to publish the finished post.</p>
                        <p>And then there's the post-publish ritual: Somewhere between 10 seconds and 10 hours later, I spot the typos. Every blogger does this. Don't let AI ruin that experience of post-publish-typo-spotting!</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Do you have an ideal creative environment? Also do you believe the physical space influences your creativity?</h3>
                        <p>I need it to be quiet. That's it. I need to focus on what I write and how the story evolves on screen. It doesn't matter if I'm in my studio, in the living room or somewhere in a coworking space. A physical space doen't influence my creativity. I've been blogging for so long, I don't need a specific creative environment to get me started. Just the energy, time and half of an idea.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>A question for the techie readers: can you run us through your tech stack?</h3>
                        <p>Right now, everything runs on <a href="https://micro.blog/" rel="noopener">Micro.blog</a>. It's a Hugo based blog with some specifics for the Micro.blog service but that's it. Locally I use Obsidian to write, with the <a href="https://github.com/otaviocc/obsidian-microblog" rel="noopener">Micro.publish-plugin</a> from <a href="https://otavio.cc/" rel="noopener">Ot&aacute;vio</a>. I also use <a href="https://getdrafts.com/" rel="noopener">Drafts</a> for shorter posts sometimes, in which I use <a href="https://actions.getdrafts.com/a/2OQ" rel="noopener">an action</a> to publish directly on my site.</p>
                        <p>For images and screenshots, I use the <a href="https://heydingus.net/shortcuts/bulk-mb-image-uploader" rel="noopener">Bulk MB Image Uploader</a> MacOS Shortcut from Jarrod Blundy's <a href="https://heydingus.net/shortcuts" rel="noopener">Heydingus Shortcuts Library</a> and tweaked it a bit. It's not a perfect setup but it works. I might vibecode a better setup in the near future with these building blocks. Maybe create my own editor with shortcuts and workflows that are tailored to my way of working.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Given your experience, if you were to start a blog today, would you do anything differently?</h3>
                        <p>I would definitely stay focused on one domain and one name. I've had so many different domain names for different types of blogs, because I thought I needed all these different platforms and focus. Sometimes it is useful, especially when I use blog software for commercial purposes. But my personal site, from the early 2000-days to now, I would try to keep it more focussed on the same domain. While changing weblog software on the background. You could say I'm <a href="https://baty.net/" rel="noopener">Jack-Baty</a>ing Light ;-) (all the love to Jack, he is pushing the possibilities of blogging software!)</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Financial question since the Web is obsessed with money: how much does it cost to run your blog? Is it just a cost, or does it generate some revenue? And what's your position on people monetising personal blogs?</h3>
                        <p>I only pay for my domains and hosting. I try to keep old domains as long as possible. The yearly costs of domains in total are &euro;55. Micro.blog is $50 a year (&euro;42). So give or take &euro;100 a year. I don't create direct revenue from the blog. But because I've been around so long it gave me an extensive network of interesting people who want to work with me on digital fitness, AI and new technology. So there are indirect revenues, which I think is the best way in the long run. If people want to monetize their personal blog, go ahead! I don't mind you sell your zine, stickers, workshop and other stuff through your blog. Just don't put ads on them. Or do it the <a href="https://www.densediscovery.com/" rel="noopener">Dense Discovery</a> way, with artisanal, value-aligned sponsors who fit in the format.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Time for some recommendations: any blog you think is worth checking out? And also, who do you think I should be interviewing next?</h3>
                        <p>I am so happy to see a renaissance of the personal internet. New search engines, cross-overs to digital gardens and personal knowledge management. That said, let me first drop some bloggers who have been around as long as the web.</p>
                        <ul>
                            <li>Dave Winer's <a href="http://scripting.com/" rel="noopener">Scripting.com</a>, the OG. The Blogfather. Without him, blogging, RSS and podcasting would not be as open as it is today.</li>
                            <li>Ton Zijlstra's <a href="https://www.zylstra.org/" rel="noopener">Interdependent Thoughts</a>, my dear friend who did keep his domain and blogging setup going for all those years.</li>
                            <li>Peter Rukavina's <a href="https://ruk.ca/" rel="noopener">blog</a>, whose posts I love to read because of his stories on Prince Edwards Island, printing, art, his family and just... life!</li>
                        </ul>
                        <p>Some others worth recommending</p>
                        <ul>
                            <li>Tracy Durnell's <a href="https://tracydurnell.com/mind-garden/" rel="noopener">Mind Garden</a>, I love her style of writing, her thinking and her weeknotes.</li>
                            <li><a href="https://www.felienne.nl/" rel="noopener">Felienne Hermans</a>, her published newsletter with critical notes on AI and education. Scroll down in an edition for the English version</li>
                            <li>Austin Kleon, his books, <a href="https://austinkleon.com/" rel="noopener">blog</a> and newsletter are interconnected. I love how Kleon works and publishes.</li>
                            <li>Mike Sass, his <a href="https://shellsharks.com/scrolls/" rel="noopener">Shellshark Scrolls</a> are a weekly roundup at the intersection of the indieweb and the fediverse.</li>
                        </ul>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Final question: is there anything you want to share with us?</h3>
                        <p>I have been quiet on my blog lately, <a href="https://tantek.com/2021/051/b1/life-happens" rel="noopener">something that happens</a> to most of us. For me, it is because of work and a sideproject I'm working on. This is called CreativeNotes, in which I interview creative professionals in the Netherlands about how they use paper notes in their creative process. I'm exploring that pivotal moment when creatives consciously choose an analog tool over a screen. I want to document how paper notes not only help bring focus and flow, but often serve as the essential building blocks of the final creative product.</p>
                        <p>By collecting stories and notebook images from a wide range of creators, I'm looking for patterns in how ideas develop on paper. What I find may be useful for anyone who thinks for a living.</p>
                        <p>You can learn more about the project (in Dutch) here: <a href="https://notes.frankmeeuwsen.com/over-creativenotes" rel="noopener">https://notes.frankmeeuwsen.com/over-creativenotes</a></p>
                    </section>
                </section>

                <!-- Closing -->
                <p>&bull;--&#9825;--&bull;</p>

            </section>
]]></content:encoded>
      <pubDate>Fri, 10 Apr 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid isPermaLink="true">https://zacharykai.net/notes/pb/meeuwsen</guid>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>People and Blogs: Anthony Nelzin-Santos</title>
      <link>https://zacharykai.net/notes/pb/anthony</link>
      <description>People and Blogs is a series by Manuel Moreale featuring the people behind personal blogs and the stories of their corners of the web. This conversation is with Anthony Nelzin-Santos. Do go visit thei...</description>
      <content:encoded><![CDATA[<section class="e-content">

                <!-- Introduction -->
                <p id="top" class="p-summary"><em><a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/pb" rel="noopener">People and Blogs</a> is a series by <a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/" rel="noopener">Manuel Moreale</a> featuring the people behind personal blogs and the stories of their corners of the web. This conversation is with Anthony Nelzin-Santos. Do go visit <a href="https://z1nz0l1n.com" rel="noopener">their blog</a> and say hello!</em></p>

                <!-- Interview -->
                <section>
                    <h2>Interview</h2>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Let&rsquo;s start from the basics: can you introduce yourself?</h3>
                        <p><em>Bonjour !</em> I&rsquo;m a militant wayfarer, budding typographer, pathological reader, slow cyclist, obsessive tinkerer, dangerous cook, amateur bookbinder, homicidal gardener, mediocre sewist, and fanatical melomaniac living in Lyon (France). I was a technology journalist and journalism teacher for sixteen years, but i now work in instructional design.</p>
                        <p>In my spare time, i take <a href="https://archityp.es/" rel="noopener">photos of old storefronts</a> to preserve a rapidly fading typographical tradition. One of these days, i&rsquo;ll finally finish the typefaces i&rsquo;ve been working on forever. And my novel. And the painting of the bathroom. (My wife is a saint.)</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>What&rsquo;s the story behind your blog?</h3>
                        <p>I was born a few years before the web was invented and grew up at this fascinating time when everybody wanted to do something with it, but nobody knew quite what yet. We were still supposed to learn Logo and Pascal in technology class, but most of the teachers understood the importance of the web and taught us the basics of HTML and CSS. I built my first website in 2000&hellip; as a school assignment!</p>
                        <p>By 2007, i was one of those insufferable tech bloggers who made enough money to feel entitled, but not enough to feel safe. (I moonlighted as a graphic designer.) When more established outlets came knocking at my door, i shut down my blog and became one of those insufferable tech journalists who make enough money to feel entitled, but not enough to feel safe. (I moonlighted as a journalism teacher.)</p>
                        <p>I kept a personal blog under the &ldquo;zinzolin&rdquo; moniker. <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinzolin" rel="noopener">This shade of purple</a> is my favourite colour, partly because it sounds a bit like my name. Over the years, it became more and more difficult to find the energy to write recreationally after having spent the day writing professionally. In 2025, feeling more than a little burnt out, i rebooted my blog and switched from French to English. Fortunately, the name is equally weird in both languages.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>What does your creative process look like when it comes to blogging?</h3>
                        <p>I don&rsquo;t have a process so much as a way of managing the incessant chatter in my head. I write to give myself the permission to forget, and i publish to gift myself the ability to remember. You&rsquo;ll never catch me without some way to capture those little &ldquo;brain itches&rdquo; &mdash; a notebook, the <a href="https://apps.apple.com/app/bloom-notes-daily-writing/id6443783029" rel="noopener">Bloom</a> app, a digital recorder, the back of my hand&hellip; (I wrote part of this interview as a long series of text messages to myself!)</p>
                        <p>In the middle of the week, i start reviewing my notes to find a common theme or extract the strongest idea. When an incomplete thought keeps coming back, i don&rsquo;t try to force it by staring at a blinking cursor. I take a long walk, and usually, i have to stop part way to write. Most of the actual blogging is done long before i sit down to properly draft my weekly note.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Do you have an ideal creative environment? Also do you believe the physical space influences your creativity?</h3>
                        <p>I have this romantic notion that the more comfortable i am, the more i can edit, the worse my writing tends to get. If i could, i&rsquo;d write everything longhand in a rickety train, stream-of-consciousness style, and publish the raw scans of my notebooks. You wouldn&rsquo;t be able to read half of it, but i can assure you the illegible half would be Nobel-prize worthy.</p>
                        <p>But then, some things only happen after a few hours of diligent editing. If i give myself enough time, i can stop transcribing my notes and start conversing with them. There&rsquo;s always something worth exploring in the gap between our past and present selves &ndash; even if the past was two days ago &ndash; but that delicate work requires a conducive environment.</p>
                        <p>Judging by my recent output, it looks like this environment comprises <a href="https://www.vitsoe.com/eu/620" rel="noopener">a good chair</a>, a MacBook Air on one of those ugly lap desks, <a href="https://github.com/anthonynelzinsantos/QWeuRTY" rel="noopener">my custom international QWERTY layout</a>, <a href="https://ia.net/writer" rel="noopener">iA Writer</a> for writing and <a href="https://www.antidote.info/en/" rel="noopener">Antidote</a> for proofreading, cosy lighting, just the right amount of background noise, and most important of all, a pot of delicious coffee.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>A question for the techie readers: can you run us through your tech stack?</h3>
                        <p>I&rsquo;ve tried pretty much every CMS and SSG under the sun, but i&rsquo;ve always come back to WordPress, until Matt Mullenweg reminded us that a benevolent dictator <a href="https://www.theverge.com/2024/9/27/24256361/wordpress-wp-engine-drama-explained-matt-mullenweg" rel="noopener">still is a dictator</a>. <em>Z1NZ0L1N</em> is now built on <a href="https://ghost.org/" rel="noopener">Ghost</a> and hosted by <a href="https://www.magicpages.co?aff=28KZ2RKopuJG" rel="noopener">Magic Pages</a>.</p>
                        <p>I used to use <a href="https://tinylytics.app" rel="noopener">Tinylytics</a> and <a href="https://buttondown.com" rel="noopener">Buttondown</a>, but i&rsquo;m now using Ghost&rsquo;s integrated analytics and newsletter features. My other websites are hosted on a VPS with <a href="https://www.infomaniak.com/goto/fr/home?utm_term=5fd3bff1d1501" rel="noopener">Infomaniak</a>, which is also where i get my domain names, e-mail, and assorted cloud services.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Given your experience, if you were to start a blog today, would you do anything differently?</h3>
                        <p>That&rsquo;s a question i had to ask myself when i rebooted <em>Z1NZ0L1N</em> last year. I switched to English in a bid to better separate my professional output from my recreational output. I jettisoned most of my audience, but i found a new community around the <a href="https://indieweb.org/IndieWeb_Carnival" rel="noopener">IndieWeb Carnival</a> and quickly rebuilt a readership on my own merits. I get excited each time i get an e-mail from someone i don&rsquo;t know from a country on the other side of the globe.</p>
                        <p>I wanted to find a way to publish regularly without turning <em>Z1NZ0L1N</em> into the umpteenth link blog. After a few experiments, i&rsquo;ve settled on a weekly note that&rsquo;s part &ldquo;what i&rsquo;m doing&rdquo;, part &ldquo;what the rest of the world is doing&rdquo;. This is old-school blogging meets recommendation algorithms &mdash; and i love it.</p>
                        <p>Some things haven&rsquo;t changed, though, and will never change. I use an open-source CMS that i could host myself, not a proprietary platform that i can&rsquo;t control. I designed my theme myself. I don&rsquo;t play the SEO/GEO game.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Financial question since the Web is obsessed with money: how much does it cost to run your blog? Is it just a cost, or does it generate some revenue? And what&rsquo;s your position on people monetising personal blogs?</h3>
                        <p>I pay a little less than &euro;10/month for Magic Pages&rsquo; starter plan with the custom themes add-on. Considering that it saves me &euro;15/month in third-party services, i&rsquo;d say it&rsquo;s a fair price. I pay &euro;12/year for the <code>z1nz0l1n.com</code> domain, but i also registered a few variations, including <code>zinzolin.fr</code>, which was first registered in 1999! Blogging is my least expensive hobby &mdash; by far.</p>
                        <p>As someone who&rsquo;s worked a lot on the economics of independent publishing, i&rsquo;m happily subscribed to a few news outlets and magazines. I like the idea of $1/month memberships for blogs, but in practice, i find it hard to track multiple micro-subscriptions on top of my existing (and frankly far too numerous) digital subscriptions.</p>
                        <p>I wonder if we should create blogging collectives, almost like unions and coops, to collect and redistribute a single subscription in between members. In the meantime, i&rsquo;ll continue not talking about <a href="https://ko-fi.com/z1nz0l1n" rel="noopener">my Ko-Fi page</a>.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Time for some recommendations: any blog you think is worth checking out? And also, who do you think I should be interviewing next?</h3>
                        <p><a href="https://theforest.link" rel="noopener">The Forest</a> and <a href="https://chronosaur.us/" rel="noopener">Ye Olde Blogroll</a> are fantastic discovery tools. A lot of my favourite bloggers have already been featured in <em>People and blogs</em>: VH Belvadi, BSAG, Frank Chimero, Keenan, Piper Haywood, Nick Heer, Tom McWright, Riccardo Mori, Jim Nielsen, Kev Quirk, Arun Venkatesan, Zinzy&hellip; I&rsquo;d love to see how <a href="https://v7.robweychert.com/blog/" rel="noopener">Rob Weychert</a>, <a href="https://chrisglass.com" rel="noopener">Chris Glass</a>, <a href="https://thenewsprint.co" rel="noopener">Josh Ginter</a> or <a href="https://melanie-richards.com" rel="noopener">Melanie Richards</a> would answer. Their approach to blogging couldn&rsquo;t be more different, but they each informed mine in their own way.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Final question: is there anything you want to share with us?</h3>
                        <p>Since 2008, i&rsquo;ve taken thousands of photos of old storefronts. It began as a way to inform my typographical practice, but it rapidly became an excuse to go out and pay attention &ndash; really pay attention &ndash; to the world around me. You wouldn&rsquo;t believe the things i&rsquo;ve discovered in side streets, the number of conversations i&rsquo;ve struck after taking a picture of a once-beloved shop, and how my way of looking at the evolution of cities has entirely changed.</p>
                        <p>If you&rsquo;re up for a little challenge, find your own collection. It might be cool doors, weird postboxes, triangular things, every <a href="https://www.everybookshopinnovascotia.com" rel="noopener">bookshop in Nova Scotia</a>, sewer manholes, purple things, number signs&hellip; It&rsquo;ll give you another perspective not only when travelling in foreign places, but also on your (not so) familiar surroundings. It doesn&rsquo;t cost a penny, but it&rsquo;ll pay off immensely.</p>
                    </section>
                </section>

                <!-- Closing -->
                <p>&bull;--&#9825;--&bull;</p>

            </section>
]]></content:encoded>
      <pubDate>Fri, 03 Apr 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid isPermaLink="true">https://zacharykai.net/notes/pb/anthony</guid>

    <item>
      <title>People and Blogs: Nikhil Anand</title>
      <link>https://zacharykai.net/notes/pb/nikhil</link>
      <description>People and Blogs is a series by Manuel Moreale featuring the people behind personal blogs and the stories of their corners of the web. This conversation is with Nikhil Anand. Do go visit their blog an...</description>
      <content:encoded><![CDATA[<section class="e-content">

                <!-- Introduction -->
                <p id="top" class="p-summary"><em><a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/pb" rel="noopener">People and Blogs</a> is a series by <a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/" rel="noopener">Manuel Moreale</a> featuring the people behind personal blogs and the stories of their corners of the web. This conversation is with Nikhil Anand. Do go visit <a href="https://nikhil.io" rel="noopener">their blog</a> and say hello!</em></p>

                <!-- Interview -->
                <section>
                    <h2>Interview</h2>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Let's start from the basics: can you introduce yourself?</h3>
                        <p>Hi I'm Nikhil! I grew up the UAE and came to the United States for college and graduated with a degree in biomedical engineering. I worked in <a href="https://ivr.uiowa.edu/" rel="noopener">academia</a> and <a href="https://www.corteva.com/" rel="noopener">industry</a> for about 15 years before deciding to turn my attention and energies towards problems in healthcare. I'm now a graduate student at Columbia University's Medical Center and am studying clinical informatics and loving the magnificent beehive that is New York City. With the time I have, I love going to art museums, practicing calligraphy, reading short stories and graphic novels, and watching every suspense/mystery show or movie I can (huge fan of the genre; for example I've watched all of <em>Columbo</em> at least three times). I'm also trying to learn CAD and have 3D printed several small abominations.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>What's the story behind your blog?</h3>
                        <p>I started blogging around 2003 after discovering blogs like Kottke.org, <a href="https://zeldman.com/" rel="noopener">Jeffrey Zeldman's blog</a>, Greg Storey's <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20040610104158/http://www.airbag.ca/" rel="noopener">Airbag.ca</a>, and Todd Dominey's <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20050829190109/http://www.whatdoiknow.org/" rel="noopener">WhatDoIKnow.org</a>. My first blog was at <a href="https://freeorange.net/" rel="noopener">freeorange.net</a> which I now use as a placeholder for my tiny LLC's future site.</p>
                        <p>I used to live in Ames, Iowa at the time and decided to and blog what I knew, about stuff going on in the town: gossip, lectures and shows I'd attended, photos of random scenes and events, and so on. That last part proved to be great: I'd hear from a quite a few alumni or former residents who'd have photo requests for nostalgia and I'd gladly oblige, especially since I was super excited to use my first digital camera, a whopping 5 megapixel Sony DSC-F717 &#128522;</p>
                        <p>I then stopped blogging for about 10 or so years and resumed in 2018. My current blog is essentially a freeform dump: just this m&eacute;lange of stuff I find interesting and/or may want to reference later. There's really no audience in mind. I use a lot of tags on my posts and am often delighted by exploring them a while later. I moved all my <a href="https://nikhil.io/bookmarks/" rel="noopener">bookmarks</a> over from PinBoard (an excellent service) and am trying to <a href="https://nikhil.io/photos/" rel="noopener">get off Instagram</a>. I'm also trying to be better about making and sharing things (photos, calligraphy, art) no matter how terrible they are and not just consuming them.</p>
                        <p>As for the name, I really wanted a domain hack, <code>www.nikh.il</code>, but this sadly required permission from the Israeli government I was pretty sure I wouldn't get &#128517; So I went with the shortest and 'coolest' TLD I could find and ended up with nikhil.io. I also have <a href="https://nikhil.fish/" rel="noopener">nikhil.fish</a> as an alias for no reason.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>What does your creative process look like when it comes to blogging?</h3>
                        <p>I think half my site's half a <a href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/tumblelog" rel="noopener">a tumblelog</a>. As for the other half, I have a Markdown file called <code>log.md</code> in my iCloud Drive that I dump inchoate thoughts into (it's at about half a meg right now). I also use the excellent <a href="https://culturedcode.com/things/" rel="noopener">Things</a> app on my phone to save blog posts, names, recommendations, articles, and media of interest to peruse later. When I have time, I look at these two sources to post and comment on something I think is beautiful, interesting, or funny.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Do you have an ideal creative environment? Also do you believe the physical space influences your creativity?</h3>
                        <p>All professional creatives I know personally have a space that they attend to do their work and they have told me that this matters immensely to them. In my case, I have <a href="https://nikhil.io/uses/" rel="noopener">a setup</a> I've used reliably over many years and love it. I especially love my sit-to-stand desk (on wheels), giant display, and clickity-clack keyboard. I always listen to ambient music or white noise while working on anything (<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loscil" rel="noopener">Loscil</a>'s works are a favorite).</p>
                        <p>I've found that I just cannot focus in coffeehouses or libraries. And I absolutely cannot work or think in harsh "cool white" lighting (3000K or lower; if you need me to divulge secrets, just put me in a room with two tubelights for thirty seconds). I know a lot of people (like <a href="https://catherineknepper.com/" rel="noopener">my wife</a>, a writer) who can work anywhere and may be a bit envious. I am also in the habit of pacing around and muttering things to myself while working and these are not nice things to do at coffeehouses or libraries.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>A question for the techie readers: can you run us through your tech stack?</h3>
                        <p>I write all my posts in Markdown and use an old and heavily modded version of <a href="https://www.11ty.dev/" rel="noopener">11ty.js</a> with several <a href="https://github.com/markdown-it/markdown-it" rel="noopener">Markdown-it</a> plugins and supported by quite a few <code>bash</code> and Node scripts to generate the HTML pages. Images are processed with <a href="https://sharp.pixelplumbing.com/" rel="noopener">Sharp</a>. The blog theme is a mess of TSX and SASS files. All posts and code are in <code>git</code> and Github. I build everything on my laptop and sync all the files to an S3 bucket that serves my blog through CloudFront.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Given your experience, if you were to start a blog today, would you do anything differently?</h3>
                        <p>Not really. I've spent enough time monkeying with the design/structure and code where my setup fits my needs like a bespoke suit. You can always nerd out over tooling, and it's a lot of fun, but I've suspended that in favor of using the tools. For the time being at least &#128517;</p>
                        <p>Now if my wife or a friend were starting a blog, I would absolutely recommend a platform like <a href="https://bearblog.dev/" rel="noopener">Bear</a>. Anything simple, hosted, not creepy, and not run by greedy and/or awful people.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Financial question since the Web is obsessed with money: how much does it cost to run your blog? Is it just a cost, or does it generate some revenue? And what's your position on people monetising personal blogs?</h3>
                        <p>It costs ~$5 a month. A giant part of that cost is the domain name. Zero revenue. No plans on 'growing' it or whatever; it's just my little garden on the internet.</p>
                        <p>I have no problem with people monetising their blogs as long as the strategy they employ is respectful to visitors' privacy and unobtrusive to their experience. Patronage/memberships aside, <a href="https://techcrunch.com/2017/03/29/r-i-p-the-deck/" rel="noopener">The Deck</a> comes to mind as an ad platform that achieved both these things very well.</p>
                        <p>I do have my problems with platforms like Substack and might write a blog post about this later.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Time for some recommendations: any blog you think is worth checking out? And also, who do you think I should be interviewing next?</h3>
                        <p>Please interview <a href="https://chrisglass.com/" rel="noopener">Chris Glass</a>! His lovely and popular blog is a huge inspiration for mine, layout and content, and he's been at it since at least 2003 IIRC. Another old favorite is <a href="https://www.witoldriedel.com/" rel="noopener">Witold Riedel's log</a>. I'm also really digging <a href="https://%E3%83%9E%E3%83%AA%E3%82%A6%E3%82%B9.com/" rel="noopener">this blog</a> I discovered recently.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Final question: is there anything you want to share with us?</h3>
                        <p>I just put up <a href="https://nikhil.io/art/" rel="noopener">a small project</a> I've wanted to do for a while, my own little curated digital gallery of art I've loved over the years. It was mostly a design exercise but I thought I might use some LLM to discover some themes in why I love these works (or maybe you just love looking at things and don't really need to understand why).</p>
                        <p>Other than that, I am so happy with what feels to me like a resurgence in personal blogging (here's <a href="https://hnpwd.github.io/" rel="noopener">a recent index</a> of personal blogs from readers of HackerNews). Thank you for having me in your beautiful space and featuring several other lovely and interesting people! This is a fantastic project Manu &#129303;</p>
                    </section>
                </section>

                <!-- Closing -->
                <p>&bull;--&#9825;--&bull;</p>

            </section>
]]></content:encoded>
      <pubDate>Fri, 27 Mar 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid isPermaLink="true">https://zacharykai.net/notes/pb/nikhil</guid>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>People and Blogs: Melanie Richards</title>
      <link>https://zacharykai.net/notes/pb/melanie</link>
      <description>People and Blogs is a series by Manuel Moreale featuring the people behind personal blogs and the stories of their corners of the web. This conversation is with Melanie Richards. Do go visit their blo...</description>
      <content:encoded><![CDATA[<section class="e-content">

                <!-- Introduction -->
                <p id="top" class="p-summary"><em><a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/pb" rel="noopener">People and Blogs</a> is a series by <a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/" rel="noopener">Manuel Moreale</a> featuring the people behind personal blogs and the stories of their corners of the web. This conversation is with Melanie Richards. Do go visit <a href="https://melanie-richards.com/blog/" rel="noopener">their blog</a> and say hello!</em></p>

                <!-- Interview -->
                <section>
                    <h2>Interview</h2>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Let's start from the basics: can you introduce yourself?</h3>
                        <p>I&rsquo;m a Group Product Manager co-leading the core product at Webflow, i.e. helping teams visually design and build websites. My personal mission is to empower people to make inspiring, impactful, and inclusive things on the web. That&rsquo;s been the through line of my career so far: I started out as a designer at a full-service agency called Fuzzco, moved to the web platform at Microsoft Edge, continued building for developers at Netlify, and am now aiming to make web creation even more democratic with the Webflow platform.</p>
                        <p>I transitioned from design to product management while at Microsoft Edge. I wanted to take part in steering the future of the web platform, instead of remaining downstream of those decisions. I feel so lucky to have worked on new features in HTML, ARIA, CSS, and JavaScript with other PMs and developers in the W3C and WHATWG.</p>
                        <p>I&rsquo;m a builder at heart, so I love to work on <a href="https://melanie-richards.com/projects/" rel="noopener">webby side projects</a> as well as a whole bevy of analog hobbies: knitting, sewing, weaving, sketchbooking, and journaling.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>What's the story behind your blog?</h3>
                        <p>I have a couple primary blogs right now:</p>
                        <ul>
                            <li>melanie-richards.com/blog, simply the blog that lives at my main website. I post here about the web, design, development, accessibility, product management, etc. One practice I&rsquo;ve been keeping for a few years now is my monthly Learning Log. These posts are a compendium of what I&rsquo;ve been shipping or making, what I&rsquo;ve been learning, side quests, neat links around the internet, and articles I&rsquo;ve been reading. When I&rsquo;m in a particularly busy period (as was the case in 2025; my first child was born in September), this series is my most consistent blogging practice.</li>
                            <li><a href="https://making.melanie-richards.com" rel="noopener">making.melanie-richards.com</a>: this is the blog where I post about my aforementioned analog projects. Quite a lot of sewing over the past year!</li>
                        </ul>
                        <p>From 2013&ndash;2016 I also had a blog and directory called Badass Lady Creatives (wish I had spent more than five minutes on the name, haha). This featured women who were doing cool things in various &ldquo;creative&rdquo; industries. At the time it seemed like every panel, conference lineup, and group project featured all or mostly dudes. The blog was a way to push back on that a little bit and highlight people who were potentially overlooked. Since then gender representation (for one) seems to have gotten a bit better in these industries. But the work and joy of celebrating diverse, inspiring talent is never done!</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>What does your creative process look like when it comes to blogging?</h3>
                        <p>Big &ldquo;yeet to production&rdquo; vibes for me! I use Obsidian to scribble down my thoughts and write an initial draft. Obsidian creates Markdown files, so I copy and paste those into Visual Studio Code (my code editor), add some images and make some tweaks, and then push to production. I really try not to overthink it <em>too</em> much. However, I will admit that I have a tons of drafts in Obsidian that never see the light of day. It can be cathartic enough just to scribble it down, even if I never publish the thought.</p>
                        <p>For my Learning Log posts, I use <a href="https://melanie-richards.com/blog/speeding-up-learning-logs/" rel="noopener">a Readwise =&gt; Obsidian workflow I describe in this blog post</a>. Reader by Readwise is the app where I store and read all my RSS feeds and newsletter forwards.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>Do you have an ideal creative environment? Also do you believe the physical space influences your creativity?</h3>
                        <p>&ldquo;Parallel play&rdquo; is the biggest, most joyful boon to my creativity. I love to be in the company of others as we independently work on our own projects side by side.</p>
                        <p>There&rsquo;s a delicate balance when it comes to working on creative projects socially. For example, my mom, my aunt, and I often have Sew Day over FaceTime on Sundays. Everyone&rsquo;s pretty committed to what they&rsquo;re working on, so it&rsquo;s easy to sew and talk and sing (badly &#128514;) at the same time. I also used to go to a local craft night that very sadly disbanded when the host shop changed hands.</p>
                        <p>For writing or coding, that takes a bit more mental focus for me. I started a Discord server with a few friends, which is dedicated to working on blog posts and side projects. We meet up once a month to talk about our projects (and shoot the breeze, usually about web accessibility and/or the goodness of dogs). Then we all log off the voice channel to go do the thing!</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
                        <h3>A question for the techie readers: can you run us through your tech stack?</h3>
                        <p>Both of these blogs use Eleventy and plain ol&rsquo; Markdown, and are hosted on Netlify. Some of my other <a href="https://melanie-richards.com/projects/" rel="noopener">side projects</a> use a content management system (CMS) like Webflow&rsquo;s CMS, or Contentful + Eleventy. Again, Webflow is my current employer.</p>
                        <p>I use a Netlify form for comments on my &ldquo;Making&rdquo; blog, and Webmentions for my main blog. I will probably pull out Webmentions from that code base: conceptually they&rsquo;ve never really &ldquo;landed&rdquo; for me, and it would be nice to delete a ton of code.</p>
                    </section>

                    <section>
